What should I learn before HTTPS, including its foundational prerequisite?

evidence_diagnostics.excerpt:
HTTPS carries HTTP messages over TLS. To understand HTTPS, study TLS first and
HTTP before TLS. This makes HTTP a foundational prerequisite two steps before
HTTPS. HTTPS protects traffic between browser and server against passive reading
and modification in transit. It does not repair application authorization bugs, prevent a
malicious server from storing data, or guarantee that a website is honest.

Document access control enforces ownership or sharing rules on every operation
involving a document. Its direct prerequisite is authorization; authentication is the
foundational prerequisite before authorization. Protect vector searches and graph
traversals with the same document scope used for PDF previews. Guessing an upload
identifier must never grant access. HTTPS protects transport, but it cannot replace
these resource permission checks.

HTTP defines requests and responses between a client and a server. A request
contains a method, target, headers, and sometimes a body. A response contains a
status code, headers, and optionally a body. HTTP itself does not encrypt the
message. In this course, HTTP is a prerequisite for understanding TLS in web
communication, and TLS is a prerequisite for understanding HTTPS. Learn this
sequence: HTTP, then TLS, then HTTPS.

TLS protects data in transit using encryption and integrity checks. A certificate helps
the client authenticate the server during the handshake. A browser checks that the
certificate matches the requested hostname and chains to a trusted authority. TLS
does not decide whether a signed-in user can read a particular document. HTTP is a
prerequisite for studying TLS in this web course; TLS is a prerequisite for HTTPS.

Authorization evaluates whether a caller may perform an action on a resource. For a
private PDF, compare the verified caller identity with the document owner or an explicit
sharing rule. Authentication is a prerequisite for authorization. Authorization is a
prerequisite for document access control. These checks belong on the server and
must cover previews, retrieval, downloads, deletion, and graph queries, even if the
interface hides buttons.

Authentication establishes the identity of a caller using credentials or an existing
session. Authorization decides whether that identity may perform a specific action on a
resource. In this course authentication is a prerequisite for authorization, and
authorization is a prerequisite for document access control. A successful login alone
does not grant permission to every PDF in an application.

Phishing uses deceptive messages or websites to persuade a person to disclose
credentials or perform an unsafe action. A message may manufacture urgency to
discourage checking the sender. Verify unexpected requests through a separate
trusted channel. HTTPS can encrypt a phishing website's traffic, so a secure
connection is not proof that the operator is trustworthy. This lesson distinguishes
transport protection from human deception.

A signed session cookie lets a server detect tampering and verify an expiry time.
HttpOnly prevents page JavaScript from reading the cookie; Secure restricts
transmission to HTTPS. A signature provides integrity, not secrecy, so session
contents must not include secrets that require encryption. A stateless signed cookie
does not by itself create per-user document ownership or provide instant revocation
without additional state.

An HTTP 401 response means authentication is required or the supplied credentials
are not accepted. An HTTP 403 response means the request is forbidden; it can occur
even when identity is known. HTTP 429 indicates too many requests and can include
a Retry-After header. HTTP 503 indicates that a service is temporarily unavailable.
Clients should distinguish these cases rather than report every failure as an invalid
password.

HTTP caching reuses a stored response when its freshness rules permit.
Cache-Control can specify private responses or prohibit storage with no-store. An
ETag is a validator that can support conditional requests and avoid downloading an
unchanged representation. Never assume a shared cache may safely store a
personalized response. This response cache differs from a database index, which
accelerates locating rows without storing an HTTP response.

Why cannot a PostgreSQL rollback remove partial Qdrant writes?

evidence_diagnostics.excerpt:
Compensating cleanup removes partial derived artifacts after a workflow fails across
services. A PostgreSQL rollback cannot erase points already written to Qdrant. Delete
by the exact upload identifier and preserve authoritative metadata until cleanup can be
retried. Cleanup is not a distributed atomic transaction: it can also fail, so record the
failure and keep operations idempotent.

A database transaction groups related changes into a unit that commits or rolls back.
For a document workflow, authoritative metadata can record which processing stage
completed. A SQL transaction does not automatically roll back writes made to an
external vector database or object store. In this course transactions are a prerequisite
for idempotency, and idempotency is a prerequisite for safe retries.

Safe retries repeat a transiently failed operation under a bounded attempt budget.
Their direct prerequisite is idempotency, whose prerequisite is transactions. Use a
delay or backoff when a provider is busy and stop retrying permanent input errors. If
an earlier write may already have succeeded, deterministic identifiers help make the
next attempt safe. Blindly repeating a non-idempotent action can duplicate data or
effects.

DNS resolves domain names to records such as IP addresses. A resolver can reuse a
cached answer until its time to live expires. A DNS lookup does not prove that an
application is healthy. After locating a server, the browser still needs a successful
connection and an HTTP response. DNS caching and HTTP caching operate at
different layers: one reuses name resolution results, the other reuses application
responses.

HTTP caching reuses a stored response when its freshness rules permit.
Cache-Control can specify private responses or prohibit storage with no-store. An
ETag is a validator that can support conditional requests and avoid downloading an
unchanged representation. Never assume a shared cache may safely store a
personalized response. This response cache differs from a database index, which
accelerates locating rows without storing an HTTP response.

Idempotency means repeating an operation has the same intended effect as
performing it once. Deterministic chunk identifiers and upserts can prevent a repeated
ingestion attempt from creating duplicate vectors. Transactions are a prerequisite for
studying idempotency in this workflow, and idempotency is a prerequisite for safe
retries. Idempotency does not mean every attempt succeeds; the operation must still
report failures.

A signed session cookie lets a server detect tampering and verify an expiry time.
HttpOnly prevents page JavaScript from reading the cookie; Secure restricts
transmission to HTTPS. A signature provides integrity, not secrecy, so session
contents must not include secrets that require encryption. A stateless signed cookie
does not by itself create per-user document ownership or provide instant revocation
without additional state.

pressure in bar. Stop operation if the measured pressure exceeds this limit. Use the
specification for this exact equipment identifier; limits for other equipment do not apply.

Equipment identifier PMP-104. The approved maximum operating pressure is 11.0 bar.
Record pressure in bar. Stop operation if the measured pressure exceeds this limit. Use the
specification for this exact equipment identifier; limits for other equipment do not apply.

Equipment identifier PMP-102. The approved maximum operating pressure is 14.0 bar.
Record pressure in bar. Stop operation if the measured pressure exceeds this limit. Use the

failure and keep operations idempotent.

effects.

evidence_diagnostics.excerpt:
Authentication establishes the identity of a caller using credentials or an existing
session. Authorization decides whether that identity may perform a specific action on a
resource. In this course authentication is a prerequisite for authorization, and
authorization is a prerequisite for document access control. A successful login alone
does not grant permission to every PDF in an application.

A signed session cookie lets a server detect tampering and verify an expiry time.
HttpOnly prevents page JavaScript from reading the cookie; Secure restricts
transmission to HTTPS. A signature provides integrity, not secrecy, so session
contents must not include secrets that require encryption. A stateless signed cookie
does not by itself create per-user document ownership or provide instant revocation
without additional state.

Authorization evaluates whether a caller may perform an action on a resource. For a
private PDF, compare the verified caller identity with the document owner or an explicit
sharing rule. Authentication is a prerequisite for authorization. Authorization is a
prerequisite for document access control. These checks belong on the server and
must cover previews, retrieval, downloads, deletion, and graph queries, even if the
interface hides buttons.

Document access control enforces ownership or sharing rules on every operation
involving a document. Its direct prerequisite is authorization; authentication is the
foundational prerequisite before authorization. Protect vector searches and graph
traversals with the same document scope used for PDF previews. Guessing an upload
identifier must never grant access. HTTPS protects transport, but it cannot replace
these resource permission checks.

TLS protects data in transit using encryption and integrity checks. A certificate helps
the client authenticate the server during the handshake. A browser checks that the
certificate matches the requested hostname and chains to a trusted authority. TLS
does not decide whether a signed-in user can read a particular document. HTTP is a
prerequisite for studying TLS in this web course; TLS is a prerequisite for HTTPS.

HTTPS carries HTTP messages over TLS. To understand HTTPS, study TLS first and
HTTP before TLS. This makes HTTP a foundational prerequisite two steps before
HTTPS. HTTPS protects traffic between browser and server against passive reading
and modification in transit. It does not repair application authorization bugs, prevent a
malicious server from storing data, or guarantee that a website is honest.

An HTTP 401 response means authentication is required or the supplied credentials
are not accepted. An HTTP 403 response means the request is forbidden; it can occur
even when identity is known. HTTP 429 indicates too many requests and can include
a Retry-After header. HTTP 503 indicates that a service is temporarily unavailable.
Clients should distinguish these cases rather than report every failure as an invalid
password.

A database transaction groups related changes into a unit that commits or rolls back.
For a document workflow, authoritative metadata can record which processing stage
completed. A SQL transaction does not automatically roll back writes made to an
external vector database or object store. In this course transactions are a prerequisite
for idempotency, and idempotency is a prerequisite for safe retries.

Rate limits bound the number of requests a caller may make in a time window.
Expensive AI operations can have a smaller budget than read-only metadata requests.
HTTP 429 can tell a client to slow down. Rate limits control consumption but do not
establish identity or document ownership. A shared reviewer code often maps all
reviewers to one shared request budget and shared workspace.

HTTP caching reuses a stored response when its freshness rules permit.
Cache-Control can specify private responses or prohibit storage with no-store. An
ETag is a validator that can support conditional requests and avoid downloading an
unchanged representation. Never assume a shared cache may safely store a
personalized response. This response cache differs from a database index, which
accelerates locating rows without storing an HTTP response.

methodology.scope: Authored PDFs with synthetic distractors; warm local models and in-memory Qdrant brute-force search.
limitations: No hosted ANN, HTTP, concurrency, PostgreSQL, or LLM generation benchmark.
Page-label precision is not human-verified passage relevance or generated-answer accuracy.
Source fragments are checked by exact text presence, not semantic correctness.
Validation cases were used to diagnose identifier failures; fresh held-out authored cases are separate and not independently annotated.
One warm sequential run per case; not a concurrency, uptime, or production-scale guarantee.
